item.title: Testing Common Causality of Covariates: Evidence from Private-Sector Ban-the-Box Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.29148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When including covariates in Difference-in-Differences, researchers must consider not only which covariates to include, but also how to model them. The Common Causality of Covariates (CCC) assumption requires that covariate coefficients in the untreated potential-outcome model remain constant across regions and periods. Violations can bias DID estimators even when the relevant covariates are correctly included. I develop a CCC test based on Wald tests from an additive model that uses untreated observations in pre-treatment periods to assess whether covariate coefficients vary across regions, periods, or both. Motivated by this specification problem, I show theoretically that well-specified Integrated DID estimators are consistent, whereas overly restrictive models can introduce bias and, under conditional homoskedasticity, unnecessarily flexible models can reduce efficiency. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CCC test has good size and power. An application to private-sector Ban-the-Box policies finds variation across both regions and periods, with positive estimated effects on wages and occupational quality among employed private-sector workers.
item.dc:creator: Sunny R. Karim

item.title: Policy Learning with Network-Shaping Assignments
item.description: arXiv:2610.29221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many policies determine social arrangements whose effects depend on the relationships formed afterwards. We study how to learn such policies when a constrained joint action changes network formation and outcomes depend on exposures to the resulting network. Policy value integrates an outcome response over the distribution of post-assignment networks. The large number of feasible arrangements makes it difficult to evaluate policies directly from historical data. We therefore adopt a model-based approach that pools information across assignments to evaluate alternative arrangements. We characterize identification of policy values and construct plug-in estimators. Our regret bounds account for sampling variation, first-stage estimation error, and computational errors. Our applications to classroom seating and business groups illustrate predicted welfare gains from learned rules relative to random assignment.
item.dc:creator: Zhenxiao Chen, Zhiheng You

item.title: Demand Estimation for Rationally Inattentive Consumers
item.description: arXiv:2610.29600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a rational-inattention BLP (RI-BLP) model for demand estimation from aggregate market shares, allowing for endogenous prices and unobserved preference heterogeneity. We establish conditions for uniqueness of market-share inversion and construct a simulated RI-BLP GMM estimator with instrumental-variable moments and market-share constraints. Under regularity and simulation-accuracy conditions, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal as the number of markets grows, with the number of products fixed. Monte Carlo experiments show accurate recovery of mean utility coefficients, with less precise estimates of dispersion parameters. In a canned-tuna application, RI-BLP and logit yield similar average own-price elasticities. Unlike logit, the fitted RI-BLP model implies that a price increase can reduce demand even for similar products and shift demand toward the outside option.
item.dc:creator: Ruolei Zhu

item.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Conjoint Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.28979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Choosing an appropriate sample size is a fundamental challenge in experimental design. This challenge is particularly salient in conjoint experiments, where researchers simultaneously target many estimands whose inferential goals may be reached at different sample sizes. Conventional sample-size calculations address this challenge in an ex ante manner. In large online studies, including many conjoint experiments, data often arrive continuously, allowing researchers to dynamically stop data collection. In such settings, the relevant practical question is not "what sample size should I choose in advance?" but rather, as data accumulate, "have I learned enough yet?" A naive response is to repeatedly inspect conventional confidence intervals and $p$-values, but doing so invalidates their inferential guarantees. We address this challenge by developing a general anytime-valid framework for conjoint experiments that allows continuous monitoring and data-dependent stopping. This framework equips many common conjoint estimands with asymptotic $e$-processes, confidence sequences, and anytime-valid $p$-values, and provides a general recipe for any estimand that can be expressed as a linear contrast of population OLS coefficients. Across common conjoint settings, we demonstrate that anytime-valid inference can yield substantial sample savings relative to fixed-sample designs. The probability of early stopping frequently exceeds 50%, with mean sample savings often surpassing 25%.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Molitor, Jennah Gosciak, Michael Lindon

item.title: Bias-Aware Inference in Regularized Regression Models
item.description: arXiv:2012.14823v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider inference on a scalar regression coefficient under a constraint on the magnitude of the control coefficients. A class of estimators based on a regularized propensity score regression is shown to exactly solve a tradeoff between worst-case bias and variance. We derive confidence intervals (CIs) based on these estimators that are bias-aware: they account for the possible bias of the estimator. Under homoskedastic Gaussian errors, these estimators and CIs are near-optimal in finite samples for mean squared error and CI length. We also provide conditions for asymptotic validity of the CIs with an unknown and possibly heteroskedastic error distribution, and derive novel optimal rates of convergence under high-dimensional asymptotics that allow the number of regressors to increase more quickly than the number of observations. Extensive simulations and two empirical applications illustrate the performance of our methods.
item.dc:creator: Timothy B. Armstrong, Michal Koles\'ar, Soonwoo Kwon

item.title: Good Controls Gone Bad: Difference-in-Differences with Covariates
item.description: arXiv:2412.14447v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces the common causality of covariates (CCC) assumption in difference-in-differences with covariates. This assumption stipulates that covariates must have common effects on untreated potential outcomes across regions and periods. We also introduce Integrated Parallel Trends, a weaker alternative to conditional parallel trends that does not require point-wise equality of trends across covariate values, and can accommodate CCC violations. Pre-trend diagnostics for integrated parallel trends may reveal plausibly parallel trends that are obscured under conventional conditional parallel trends diagnostics, thereby broadening the set of empirical settings in which credible DID identification may be possible. Furthermore, we propose a new estimator called the Integrated Difference-in-Differences (DID-INT) estimator, which can identify the ATT when integrated parallel trends holds and the CCC assumption is violated. The DID-INT estimator can also accommodate treatment-effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates and compositional changes, while avoiding forbidden comparisons in staggered adoption settings.
item.dc:creator: Sunny Karim, Matthew D. Webb

item.title: Certified Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2502.17830v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hypothesis tests and confidence sets are ubiquitous in empirical research, yet their connection to subsequent decision-making is often unclear. We view statistical inference as pairing recommended decisions with guarantees of their quality---or certificates---and develop a theory of certified decisions. Specifically, we attach P-certificates---upper bounds on loss that hold with probability at least $1-\alpha$---to recommended actions. We prove that it is without loss to limit attention to P-certificates generated by minimax decisions over confidence sets, or what Manski (2021) terms "as-if decisions with a set estimate." We further show that such certificates allow safe adoption decisions for ambiguity-averse downstream decision-makers. A parallel argument applies to E-certified decisions obtained from e-values in settings with unbounded loss. We illustrate this view of statistical inference through an application to economic mobility and one to AI model routing.
item.dc:creator: Isaiah Andrews, Jiafeng Chen

item.title: Double machine learning for causal inference in a multivariate sample selection model
item.description: arXiv:2511.12640v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose double machine learning (DML) estimators of the average treatment effect (ATE) and the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) in the multivariate sample selection model with multiple ordinal selection equations. We establish asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators and study finite sample properties on simulated data. Specifically, the results of the analysis suggest that without addressing multivariate sample selection, the estimates of the causal parameters may be highly biased. However, the proposed estimators allow us to avoid these biases. Moreover, we apply the estimators to study the effect of female education on the log-wage ratio of spouses.
item.dc:creator: Sofiia Dolgikh, Bodan Potanin

item.title: Best Feasible Conditional Critical Values for a More Powerful Subvector Anderson-Rubin Test
item.description: arXiv:2601.17843v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For subvector inference in the linear instrumental variables model under homoskedasticity but allowing for weak instruments, Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2019) (GKM) propose a conditional subvector Anderson and Rubin (1949) (AR) test that uses data-dependent critical values that adapt to the strength of the parameters not under test. This test has correct size and strictly higher power than the test that uses standard asymptotic chi-square critical values. The subvector AR test is the minimum eigenvalue of a data-dependent matrix. The GKM critical value function conditions on the largest eigenvalue of this matrix. Instead, this paper considers a data-dependent critical value function that conditions on the second-smallest eigenvalue, as this eigenvalue is the appropriate indicator of weak identification. We find that the data-dependent critical value function of GKM also applies to this conditioning and show that this test has correct size and power strictly higher than the GKM test when the number of parameters not under test is larger than one. This is the best feasible test, where we consider feasible to be within the class of conditioning on a single eigenvalue. Our proposed procedure further applies to the subvector AR test statistic that is robust to an approximate Kronecker product structure of conditional heteroskedasticity as proposed by Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2024), carrying over its power advantage to this setting as well.
item.dc:creator: Jesse Hoekstra, Frank Windmeijer

item.title: Semiparametric Dynamic Logit Model with Endogenous Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.16230v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the identification and estimation of a semiparametric dynamic logit model with nonparametric link formation, in which a time-varying index of unobserved characteristics affects outcomes and links. The outcome depends on covariates, the past outcome, a fixed effect, and an unknown function of that index. Conditioning on a switch by the same agent across waves removes the fixed effect but not the change in the unknown function. When this change is common within network types and followed by a stable period, comparing two agents of the same network type, meaning they have the same probability of linking with each of the other agents, removes it and identifies covariate effects and state dependence. The pairwise conditional likelihood estimator is consistent, including when the index is continuous, and asymptotically normal when the index takes finitely many values and matches are exact. In simulations, bias falls with sample size, and coverage is near nominal among successful fits. The fixed-effects dynamic logit and pooled logits with peer-average controls remain biased when the index moves. A second estimator, conditioning on recovered network classes, is more precise. A feasibility exercise on the Glasgow Teenage Friends and Lifestyle Study examines how past use and pocket money affect adolescents' recorded tobacco or cannabis use and documents the data requirements.
item.dc:creator: Brice Romuald Gueyap Kounga

item.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
item.description: arXiv:2610.25667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two for their compliers. We discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.
item.dc:creator: Tetsuya Kaji
